id: [Were it but Me that gained the Height—]

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

World like a coat, silver clasps, ermine lined, warm with the dead inside, rolling around in the red center—I thought everything had a purpose—this was back when I still drank—and wasn’t I a special traveler, nestled in that pocket amongst the butterscotch candies, the matchbooks? Unessential but accounted for, a steady thing to touch. World like a morning glory, withered every evening, world like a bristling dog, terrified of thunder—I can’t believe how I believed, or how that belief assumed a shape around my body, taking on the imprint of my heat, gaining solidity. When anyone questioned me, I held it forth, let them touch the sleeve—I needed nothing. World like an egret, still and white on the highway divider, world like a regret typed out and then erased—I cannot hold you any closer without everyone seeing, I cannot hold you at all, it seems, your evergreens, your curling potato vine; it’s all too much much, and I a bit of goosedown, a thistle fluff, naked and hatless, unaccounted for and extra, the world like a world like a world.

The text explores a speaker's shifting, metaphor-laden relationship with "the world" through images of comfort and belief (a warm coat, a steady pocket of trinkets) contrasted with fragility and fear (a wilting flower, a thunder-shy dog), tracing a movement from a period of drinking and false certainty to a later state of doubt. prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: World, Unessential, When

outputs.L1: World like a coat, silver-clasped, ermine-lined, warm with the dead curled inside, turning over in its red center—I once believed everything had a purpose—this was back when I still drank—and wasn't I a peculiar sort of traveler, nestled in that pocket among the butterscotch candies, the matchbooks? Unessential, yet accounted for—something steady to hold onto. World like a morning glory, wilting each evening; world like a dog bristling, terrified of thunder—I can hardly believe how fully I believed, how that belief took shape around my body, molding itself to the warmth I gave off, gaining weight and form. When anyone questioned me, I offered it up, let them touch the sleeve—I needed nothing else. World like an egret, motionless and white upon the highway median; world like a regret, typed out, then deleted—I cannot hold you any closer without the whole world watching, cannot hold you at all, it seems—not your evergreens, not your curling potato vine; it is all too much, too much, and I am nothing but goosedown, a wisp of thistle, bare and hatless, unaccounted for, superfluous—the world like a world like a world.
outputs.L2:
The world resembled a coat—silver fasteners, lined in ermine, its warmth harboring something lifeless, tumbling within that crimson core. I once believed everything held meaning, back in my drinking days. Wasn't I remarkable then, tucked into that pocket beside the candy wrappers and books of matches? Not vital, but present—something reliable to reach for.

The world was also like a morning glory, collapsing each night at dusk, or like a dog with raised hackles, quaking at every thunderclap. It astonishes me now, the depth of my conviction, how that faith wrapped itself around my form, absorbing my body's warmth until it grew solid, tangible. Whenever someone doubted me, I'd offer it up, invite them to feel the fabric of my sleeve—proof that I lacked nothing.

The world became an egret too, motionless and pale against a highway median, or a confession written down then deleted. I find I cannot draw you nearer without exposing us both to watching eyes; perhaps I cannot embrace you at all—not your green pines, not your winding vine tendrils. It overwhelms me entirely, leaving me feeling like a wisp of down, a scattered seed-tuft, exposed and bare-headed, superfluous and unclaimed—the world just endless repetitions of itself, world after world after world.
outputs.L3:
The world, as the speaker renders it, refuses to hold still. It shifts from image to image like something glimpsed through rain-streaked glass: first a coat, worn close and familiar; then a morning glory, opening briefly toward the light before curling shut again; then a bristling dog, alert and unpredictable; then an egret, poised on some invisible threshold between stillness and flight; and finally a typed-then-erased regret, a thought composed and then rubbed out, leaving only the faint impression of what was almost said. These metaphors do not accumulate into a single coherent picture. Instead, they suggest a world in constant metamorphosis, one that resists being pinned down to any single meaning—much as the speaker's own understanding of their place within it refuses to settle.

This restlessness is thrown into relief by memory. The speaker recalls a former season of drinking, a blurred and heady time when everything seemed to possess purpose, when the universe itself seemed to have accounted for their presence. In that state, the speaker felt like a favored traveler, tucked snugly into the pocket of the world—small, perhaps, but chosen, protected, known. It was a feeling of belonging so complete that it needed no further justification.

That belief, the speaker recalls, was not merely an abstract comfort but something that once took on physical form. Warmed by the speaker's own body, shaped by their own heat and longing, it became solid enough to hold, tangible enough to display. It was proof—something the speaker could extend toward others as evidence that they required nothing further, that they were whole and self-sufficient, needing no external validation because they already possessed this quiet, radiant certainty of belonging.

But that solidity has not survived into the present. Now, the speaker confesses an inability to hold love or connection without immediately being exposed by it, as though intimacy itself strips away protection rather than offering it. The world's abundance—embodied in the towering permanence of evergreens, the sprawling, insistent growth of potato vines—no longer feels like a gift but an overwhelming force, too much to absorb, too much to answer. What once felt like careful accounting now feels like excess, and the speaker finds themselves unable to keep pace with such profusion.

The poem closes on an image of diminishment. Where once the speaker felt weighty enough to be tucked into the world's pocket, solid enough to be shown as proof, they now feel reduced to something almost weightless—goosedown, thistle fluff—drifting, unclaimed, uncertain of where they belong or whether they belong at all. The transformation is complete: from a traveler accounted for within the world's design to a scrap of down carried by whatever wind happens to pass, no longer sure of gravity, no longer sure of home.
outputs.L4:
**What the World Wore**

There was a time I wore the world
like a good coat, wool-thick and certain,
buttoned to the throat against whatever weather
came sniffing round the door. I kept it close.
I kept, too, a pocket full of trinkets—
small coins of belief, a compass with no needle,
a photograph worn soft at the corners—
things I touched to know that I was real,
that the ground beneath me had a name.

In those years I drank the world like whiskey,
neat, no chaser, and called the burn conviction.
I said *I understand this now* the way a man
says *I love you* to hear the shape of it
in his own mouth. I built a house of certainties
and slept well in it, dog-tired, dreamless,
the door bolted twice against the wind.

But even wool wears thin.
Even coins go dull with handling.

Somewhere in the middle years the flower in me
began to wilt—not dramatically, not all at once,
but the slow curl of petal-edge, the bowing stem,
the way a thing gives up its reaching toward the light
by degrees so small you only notice
when the whole head hangs. I flinched
at ordinary weather. I became
the dog who hears thunder in a dropped spoon,
who trembles under tables at the first
low grumble of the sky, who cannot be convinced
the storm is not always coming, is not
always about to arrive and take the roof off everything.

Doubt moved in like a tenant I couldn't evict.
It rearranged the furniture of my certainties.
It opened the pocket of trinkets and turned each one
over in its palm, asking *and this? and this?*
until the coins looked like what they were—
metal, worn, unable to purchase
anything but the illusion of purchase.

I tried to hold the world the way I used to.
I reached for the coat, the pocket, the old warm names
I'd given to the dark to make it kennel-tame.
But my hands had changed. Or the world had.
Or both of us had been pretending all along
that holding was a thing that could be done,
that a person could gather the whole
turning weight of it into two arms
and call that safety, call that home.

I can't hold it anymore.
I say this plainly now, the way you'd say
*the bone is broken* or *the well is dry*—
not with despair exactly, but with the flat
fatigue of something finally admitted.
The coat has come apart at every seam.
The trinkets have spilled and scattered
into grass I can't now find them in.

What's left is smaller than I meant to be.
What's left is goosedown, is thistle fluff,
is the pale weightless stuff that rides
whatever wind decides to lift it—
no coat, no pocket, no bolted door,
no dog to hush, no thunder to explain away.
Just this: the soft undoing of a thing
that thought itself a body, thought itself
a weight the world would have to reckon with,
now drifting, unhomed, uncertain which way
is down, which way is ground, which way
is anything at all—
and finding, in that drift, no fear worth naming,
only the strange lightness
of no longer having
to be held.
outputs.L5:
# On the World, the Unessential, and When

The world does not ask us what matters. It simply continues—turning, weathering, filling itself with noise and light—while we stand inside it trying to decide what deserves our attention. Somewhere in that effort, we begin sorting: this is necessary, this is not. This is essential, this is unessential. And yet the line between the two rarely stays where we draw it.

What we call unessential often reveals itself, later, to have been the very thing that mattered. The idle conversation, the walk taken for no reason, the hour spent doing nothing productive—these get filed away as excess, as the parts of life we could trim without loss. But when we look back, it is often these unessential moments that hold the texture of a life, the parts we remember not because they were useful but because they were *lived*.

This brings us to the question of *when*. Timing reshapes value. What seems unessential today may become essential tomorrow, and what feels urgent now may, in a year, seem barely worth the anxiety it caused. We are always making judgments from inside a moment, without knowing how that moment will look from the distance of later. The world doesn't pause to let us recalibrate; it moves, and our sense of what is essential moves with it, often only becoming clear in hindsight.

Perhaps this is the quiet lesson underneath these three words. The world is vast and indifferent to our categories. What we deem unessential is a judgment made under the pressure of a particular *when*—a specific moment, mood, or need. And because the world keeps turning, that judgment is never final. We are constantly revising what matters, discovering that the unessential of yesterday has quietly become the essential of today, and that nothing in this sorting is ever truly settled.

To live well, perhaps, is not to correctly identify what is essential once and for all, but to hold that question loosely—knowing the world will keep offering new evidence, and knowing that *when* we ask matters just as much as *what* we ask.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem that repeats the phrase "world like a" with different metaphors, exploring themes of addiction, belief, and loss.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Repetitions

You held the world like a needle you couldn't remember filling, the way morning holds its first light without asking permission. You held the world like a needle, and called it prayer because the alternative was screaming.

The world like a wound that keeps a diary. Every morning it writes the same entry in a language only scar tissue reads. You keep checking if it's healed. It answers by staying open, patient as a church with no god left inside it, just the echo of one, rattling the pews.

I held the world like a lottery ticket already lost, still folded in my pocket, still warm from being touched too many times. Hope is just heat that hasn't noticed it's leaving. I held the world like a lottery ticket and called it faith because the alternative was empty hands.

The world like a mother who left the porch light on for a house that burned down years ago. The bulb still glows. The moths still come. Nobody tells them there's nothing left to circle.

You held the world like a bottle you were saving for a special occasion that kept becoming today. Today. Today. The label peeled off from your thumbnail worrying it in the dark. What were you celebrating? The fact that you were still thirsty. The fact that thirst is the last god who never leaves.

The world like a phone that keeps ringing in a room where everyone who could answer it has already gone. You pick it up anyway. You say hello into the static and the static says your name back, garbled, almost tender, almost enough.

I held the world like a photograph left in the rain, the faces dissolving into weather, into the idea of faces, into the shape memory makes when it's trying to forgive itself for forgetting. I held the world like a photograph and called it memory because the alternative was nothing, was nothing, was the flat white absence where a face should be.

The world like a needle. The world like a wound. The world like a diary the wound keeps writing, the world like a light left on, the world like a bottle emptying itself into tomorrow's mouth—

and somewhere underneath all of it, the small persistent animal of belief, still kneeling, still asking the dark to be a door.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness piece using anaphora ("world like a...") to compare the world to various objects and animals, touching on sobriety and vulnerability.
counterfactuals.output:
# World Like A

World like a glass held too tight, knuckles white, the wine gone warm and nobody drinking anyway.

World like a dog left in the rain, not knowing which door will open, just standing there believing one will.

World like a paper cup, crushed and unfolded and crushed again, still trying to hold something.

World like a snake shedding, raw and pink underneath, everyone can see you before you're ready to be seen.

World like a chair with one short leg — you learn to sit still, to not lean too far into anything.

World like a moth that keeps finding the same bulb, scorched wings, no memory, or too much memory, same thing really.

World like a house with the lights on and no one home, or everyone home and no one speaking.

World like a fish out of water gasping in air that should be enough but isn't, not today, not like this.

World like a coin flipped and caught but never looked at, the answer suspended in a closed fist.

World like a bird that forgot how to migrate, standing in snow it wasn't built for, too proud or too tired to fly south.

World like a bottle you didn't open, sitting on the shelf like a dare, like a door, like a decision you keep almost making.

World like an old dog again — I keep coming back to the dog — waiting by the door not for food, not for walks, just for someone to remember it's there.

World like a glass, empty this time, and that's the sober truth of it: sometimes empty is the honest shape, the clean shape, the one you can actually hold without spilling.

World like a hand, open, finally, after all that gripping — just a hand, just open, just waiting to see what it's given.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical, image-heavy prose poem about someone reflecting on their past drinking and a fading relationship, using recurring metaphors for "the world."
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Bottle Held**

There was a world in every glass—amber-lit, small enough to swallow, and I drank it down like it might save me from the larger one waiting outside the door. You used to sit across the table while I built these little worlds, watched me pour continent after continent, watched me drown them one by one in my own throat.

I thought the world was something you could hold if you just found the right container. A tumbler. A marriage. Your hand, once, before it learned to flinch.

The world got smaller as the nights got longer. I made it that way—shrunk it down to the size of a shot glass, then a house, then just the space between your side of the bed and mine, which kept widening like an ocean I'd once promised to swim across for you.

You used to say I loved the bottle more than the horizon. You weren't wrong. The horizon asked nothing of me. The bottle asked nothing of me. You—you asked me to show up, to be a whole world instead of these shattered continents floating in liquor, and I couldn't. I was busy drinking the atlas. I was busy swallowing every map that might have led me back to you.

Now the world is just this: your coat gone from the hook, the quiet where your laugh used to live, ice melting in a glass I finally learned to leave untouched. The world is smaller now, but clearer—like something rinsed, like something I can almost see through.

I think about all those small drowned worlds. How I mistook oblivion for intimacy, static for stars. How you were the real world, breathing beside me, and I kept reaching instead for the false ones—the ones that fit in my palm, that dissolved by morning, that never once asked me to stay sober enough to love them back.

The world is quiet now. No glass to raise. No bottle-planet spinning its amber orbit toward my mouth. Just this bigger, harder world—the one I have to walk through sober, the one where you are not coming back, where the horizon keeps its distance, unclaimed, unswallowed, entirely and terribly real.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental short poem in prose form that uses repeated similes beginning with "world like a" to explore feelings of insignificance, belonging, and heartbreak.
counterfactuals.output:
# World Like A

World like a coin flipped and never caught, spinning its two faces—heads for insignificance, tails for the ache of wanting to matter anyway. World like a doorway you keep almost walking through, the belonging always one step past where you're standing, warm light leaking out from under a door that isn't yours to open. World like a name called out in a crowded room—not yours, but close enough that your heart lifts anyway, stupid and hopeful, before it drops back down.

World like a photograph left in the rain, the faces blurring into something that could be anyone, could be no one, could be you dissolving at the edges until insignificance feels less like drowning and more like becoming weather. World like a chair pulled up to a table that seats twelve, and you're the thirteenth, the extra, the folding chair wedged in at the corner—still fed, still there, but the wood beneath you remembers it wasn't built for this.

World like a heart-shaped locket with no photo inside, just the shape of what should be there, the absence wearing the costume of love. World like a letter you wrote and burned before sending, the smoke rising like a question no one answered. World like a hand reaching for another hand in the dark and finding only air, finding only the memory of warmth, finding out that heartbreak is just belonging in the past tense.

World like a small light in a vast field, insignificant until you remember someone, somewhere, might be looking for exactly that kind of small.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a poetic monologue that blends memory, addiction recovery, and longing, using nature and object imagery repeated through the refrain "world like a."
counterfactuals.output:
**World Like a Spoon Held to Light**

There was a river once, and I was thirsty in the wrong direction—
drinking the current instead of standing in it.
World like a spoon, tilted, always tilted,
carrying something warm that wasn't nourishment.

I remember my mother's hands smelling of cut grass and cigarettes,
how she'd say *the body keeps what the mind refuses.*
World like a jar of fireflies, forgotten on a porch rail,
their light going out one small bulb at a time
while I told myself I was only borrowing the dark.

Six months clean and the world still tastes like static—
world like a radio caught between stations,
half-song, half-nothing,
and me reaching for the dial with shaking hands
that used to reach for other things.

I think of the birch trees behind my grandfather's house,
how they'd bend in storms but never break,
white bark like scar tissue wrapped around something growing.
World like a birch tree. World like a wound that photosynthesizes.

There is a version of longing that has nothing to do with wanting the drug—
it's wanting the years back, the ordinary Tuesdays,
the smell of rain before it decides to be rain.
World like a key left in a lock that no longer fits any door I remember,
world like a match struck in wind, cupped hands, please, just this once, catch.

My sponsor says *play the tape forward*
and I do—I see the river again, but this time
I'm not drinking. I'm just standing in the cold rush of it,
letting it number my ankles, calling that arithmetic *alive.*

World like a nest after the birds have gone—
still shaped like holding, still shaped like *stay.*
World like a glass of water left on a nightstand,
untouched, patient, believing I'll come back
thirsty for something that won't unmake me.

Some mornings I wake and the light through the blinds
looks like the inside of an amber bottle,
and my whole body remembers before my mind does.
World like a scar. World like a compass losing its north
then finding, impossibly, another one.

I am learning to love the world in increments—
this spoon for cereal, not for cooking.
This match for candles, not for burning bridges I still need.
World like a birch tree bending. World like a river I no longer drink,
only wade through, slow, sober, singing something
that sounds almost like a psalm,
almost like forgiveness,
almost like the word *home*
finally landing on a tongue
that remembers how to taste
without needing
to disappear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
